claim: A compass representation was recently discovered in a neural population in the Drosophila melanogaster central complex.
source: Such a compass representation was recently discovered in a neural population in the Drosophila melanogaster central complex, a brain region implicated in spatial navigation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work, as indicated by the reference to previous research on compass representation in the fly central complex.

claim: The central complex is a brain region implicated in spatial navigation.
source: Such a compass representation was recently discovered in a neural population in the Drosophila melanogaster central complex, a brain region implicated in spatial navigation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the function of the central complex.

claim: A different neural population conjunctively encodes heading and angular velocity.
source: Here, we use two-photon calcium imaging and electrophysiology in head-fixed walking flies to identify a different neural population that conjunctively encodes heading and angular velocity, and is excited selectively by turns in either the clockwise or counterclockwise direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging and electrophysiology presented in the manuscript.

claim: This neural population is excited selectively by turns in either the clockwise or counterclockwise direction.
source: Here, we use two-photon calcium imaging and electrophysiology in head-fixed walking flies to identify a different neural population that conjunctively encodes heading and angular velocity, and is excited selectively by turns in either the clockwise or counterclockwise direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Mirror-symmetric turn responses combine with the neurons' connectivity to the compass neurons to create a mechanism for updating the fly's heading representation when the animal turns in darkness.
source: We show how these mirror-symmetric turn responses combine with the neurons' connectivity to the compass neurons to create an elegant mechanism for updating the fly's heading representation when the animal turns in darkness.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: This mechanism employs recurrent loops with an angular shift.
source: This mechanism, which employs recurrent loops with an angular shift, bears a resemblance to those proposed in theoretical models for rodent head direction cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data and modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: This mechanism bears a resemblance to those proposed in theoretical models for rodent head direction cells.
source: This mechanism, which employs recurrent loops with an angular shift, bears a resemblance to those proposed in theoretical models for rodent head direction cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to existing theoretical models in the literature.

claim: Head direction cells represent the animal's orientation with respect to a fixed external landmark.
source: In rodents, this ability is thought to rely on head direction cells, which represent the animal's orientation with respect to a fixed external landmark (Taube et al., 1990) and use vestibular signals to maintain their directional tuning in darkness (Taube, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on head direction cells.

claim: Head direction cells use vestibular signals to maintain their directional tuning in darkness.
source: In rodents, this ability is thought to rely on head direction cells, which represent the animal's orientation with respect to a fixed external landmark (Taube et al., 1990) and use vestibular signals to maintain their directional tuning in darkness (Taube, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Ring attractor models have been proposed to explain how the brain might maintain and update an internal compass representation.
source: A variety of ring attractor models — theorized networks of neurons schematized as being arranged in a ring based on their directional tuning, with connectivity strengths depending on their mutual distances — have been proposed to explain how the brain might maintain and update such an internal compass representation (Knierim and Zhang, 2012; Skaggs et al., 1995; Xie et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical modeling literature.

claim: E-PG neurons track a tethered walking fly's virtual heading in visual surroundings and in darkness.
source: In the central brain of Drosophila melanogaster, a population of neurons has been found to track a tethered walking fly's virtual heading in visual surroundings and in darkness (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: E-PG neurons reside in the central complex.
source: These neurons reside in the central complex, a brain region comprised of several distinct neuropiles, among them the donut-shaped ellipsoid body and the handle-bar-shaped protocerebral bridge (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical fact supported by the figure reference.

claim: The central complex is comprised of several distinct neuropiles, among them the donut-shaped ellipsoid body and the handle-bar-shaped protocerebral bridge.
source: These neurons reside in the central complex, a brain region comprised of several distinct neuropiles, among them the donut-shaped ellipsoid body and the handle-bar-shaped protocerebral bridge (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical knowledge and the schematic shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Dendritic calcium activity in the E-PG population localizes into a single bump that moves around the ellipsoid body as the fly turns.
source: Dendritic calcium activity in the E-PG population localizes into a single bump that moves around the ellipsoid body as the fly turns (Figure 1C–E), (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by both citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: P-EN neurons have predominantly spiny arbors in the protocerebral bridge and predominantly bouton-like projections within the ellipsoid body and noduli.
source: We will refer to these 'compass neurons' (PBG1–8.b-EBw.s-D/Vgall.b [Wolff et al., 2015]) as E-PG neurons, to signify their predominantly spiny (and, thus, putatively post-synaptic) projections within the ellipsoid body ('E-') and their predominantly bouton-like projections within the protocerebral bridge ('-P') and the gall ('G') (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data cited from Wolff et al., 2015.

claim: P-EN neurons and E-PG neurons that arborize in the same bridge glomerulus have shifted processes in the ellipsoid body.
source: However, P-EN neurons and E-PG neurons that arborize in the same bridge glomerulus have shifted processes in the ellipsoid body (compare Figure 1B and F, Wolff et al. [2015]).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1 and cited from Wolff et al., 2015.

claim: Putative P-EN axons from the left side of the bridge arborize in tiles that are shifted clockwise with respect to the E-PG wedges.
source: Putative P-EN axons from the left side of the bridge arborize in tiles that are shifted clockwise with respect to the E-PG wedges while P-EN axons from the right side of the bridge are shifted counterclockwise (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: P-EN axons from the right side of the bridge are shifted counterclockwise with respect to E-PG wedges.
source: Putative P-EN axons from the left side of the bridge arborize in tiles that are shifted clockwise with respect to the E-PG wedges while P-EN axons from the right side of the bridge are shifted counterclockwise (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: P-EN population calcium activity in the noduli of flies walking in the dark was strongly modulated by the fly's angular velocity.
source: P-EN population calcium activity in the noduli of flies walking in the dark was strongly modulated by the fly's angular velocity.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When the fly turned clockwise, P-EN activity increased in the left nodulus, and vice versa.
source: When the fly turned clockwise, P-EN activity increased in the left nodulus, and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The difference between calcium transients evoked in the two noduli was correlated to the fly's angular velocity (Pearson's R = 0.65 ± 0.14, mean ± SD, N = 10 flies, p<0.001 in all cases).
source: Thus, the difference between calcium transients evoked in the two noduli was correlated to the fly's angular velocity (Pearson's R = 0.65 ± 0.14, mean ± SD, N = 10 flies, p<0.001 in all cases, Figure 2C,D, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Noduli calcium responses were dominated by the fly's angular velocity and largely indifferent to the fly's forward speed.
source: In fact, noduli calcium responses were dominated by the fly's angular velocity and largely indifferent to the fly's forward speed, as revealed by generalized linear regression analysis (Figure 2E, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: P-EN population activity is mirror-symmetrically tuned to angular velocity, with neurons innervating the right side of the bridge preferentially responding to clockwise rotation and vice versa.
source: Thus, P-EN population activity is mirror-symmetrically tuned to angular velocity, with neurons innervating the right side of the bridge (and therefore the left nodulus) preferentially responding to clockwise rotation and vice versa, matching the requirements of our conceptual model (Figures 1H and 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data and is consistent with the conceptual model.

claim: P-ENs segregated into two anatomically defined subpopulations: Neurons with their soma in the right hemisphere increased their activity during turns to the right and decreased it during turns to the left, whereas neurons residing in the left hemisphere showed the inverse activity profile.
source: We found that P-ENs segregated into two anatomically defined subpopulations: Neurons with their soma in the right hemisphere increased their activity during turns to the right and decreased it during turns to the left, whereas neurons residing in the left hemisphere showed the inverse activity profile (Figure 3B,C and Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: P-EN responses to changes in rotational velocity were similar in darkness and visual closed loop conditions.
source: Note that P-EN responses to changes in rotational velocity were similar in darkness and visual closed loop conditions (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,D,E,H), which allowed us to pool data for all population statistics presented in Figure 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data across experimental conditions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: P-ENs were generally not tuned to forward velocity.
source: Consistent with our previous observations, P-ENs were generally not tuned to forward velocity (see Materials and methods and also Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: On average, P-EN spike rates increased by 5.6 Hz during fast turns in the preferred compared to fast turns in the non-preferred direction.
source: On average, P-EN spike rates increased by 5.6 Hz during fast turns in the preferred compared to fast turns in the non-preferred direction, but there was considerable heterogeneity across cells ('rate modulation': 5.6 ± 3.7 Hz, N = 12; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: P-EN bandwidth corresponded well with the range of rotational velocities displayed by turning flies.
source: Likewise, P-ENs were heterogeneous in the range of rotational velocities over which their activity was modulated ('P-EN bandwidth': 145 ± 82°/s, N = 12). Overall, however, P-EN bandwidth corresponded well with the range of rotational velocities displayed by turning flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of neural tuning to behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The P-EN bandwidths of the left and right P-EN subpopulations were largely overlapping.
source: We also noted that the P-EN bandwidths of the left and right P-EN subpopulations were largely overlapping (Figure 4C, left), so that the inflexion points of their tuning curves (the rotational velocities for half-maximal P-EN activation) were clustered around 0°/s (Figure 4C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When the fly is walking, the total activity of the P-EN population is roughly constant, with the contributions of the left and right P-EN subpopulations depending on the fly's momentary rotational velocity.
source: Thus, when the fly is walking, the total activity of the P-EN population is roughly constant, with the contributions of the left and right P-EN subpopulations depending on the fly's momentary rotational velocity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling/simulation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F based on experimental data.

claim: Spikes occurred well after the peak of the rotational velocity, on average by 123 ± 43 ms (N = 12).
source: Across all P-ENs, we found that spikes occurred well after the peak of the rotational velocity, on average by 123 ± 43 ms (N = 12) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-triggered average analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In all P-ENs, the maximum difference between left and right turn correlation coefficients occurred at positive temporal lags (130 ± 73 ms, N = 12).
source: In all P-ENs, the maximum difference between left and right turn correlation coefficients occurred at positive temporal lags (130 ± 73 ms, N = 12), confirming that P-EN spiking activity changed as a response to turns instead of preceding them (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by generalized linear regression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Individual P-ENs encode the fly's recent rotational velocity, with left and right P-ENs segregating into two subpopulations with mirror-symmetric tuning profiles.
source: Overall, individual P-ENs encode the fly's recent rotational velocity, with left and right P-ENs segregating into two subpopulations with mirror-symmetric tuning profiles.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the electrophysiological data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: Two-dimensional tuning maps of P-EN spike rates to rotational velocity and virtual heading revealed localized peaks in firing rate.
source: We constructed two-dimensional tuning maps of P-EN spike rates to rotational velocity and virtual heading, which revealed localized peaks in firing rate (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For each cell, tuning indices for rotation and heading were, in all but one case (p=0.0676), larger than the 95th percentile of the shuffled control distribution.
source: For each cell, we also calculated indices for rotation and heading tuning (Figure 5B, see Materials and methods), which were, in all but one case (p=0.0676), larger than the 95th percentile of the shuffled control distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: P-EN heading tuning was generally stable over time.
source: P-EN heading tuning was generally stable over time, although we occasionally observed drifts in the neuron's preferred heading angle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For all epochs recorded in flies walking with visual feedback, the P-ENs' preferred heading angles during the epochs differed by only 6 ± 5% from the average of the entire experiment (population mean, N = 4).
source: For all epochs recorded in flies walking with visual feedback, we found that the P-ENs' preferred heading angles during the epochs differed by only 6 ± 5% from the average of the entire experiment (population mean, N = 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: P-EN neurons are tuned to the fly's heading as well as the fly's rotations, both when flies walked under visual closed loop conditions and in darkness.
source: Overall, we found P-EN neurons to be tuned to the fly's heading as well as the fly's rotations, both when flies walked under visual closed loop conditions and in darkness (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: P-EN spiking was tuned to rotational velocity in non-preferred heading quadrants and to heading during non-preferred rotations.
source: Nevertheless, we found P-EN spiking to be tuned to rotational velocity in non-preferred heading quadrants and to heading during non-preferred rotations (Figure 6E left; rotation tuning at non-preferred heading angles: 2.3 ± 2.1 Hz, heading tuning during non-preferred rotations: 1.2 ± 1.1 Hz; one sample t-test: p=0.026 and p=0.043, respectively; N = 6 for both comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Tuning of P-EN output is strongly conjunctive.
source: These observations suggest not only that tuning of P-EN output is strongly conjunctive, but also that this property may be sharpened within single P-ENs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of conditional tuning curves and comparison of spike rates versus membrane potential.

claim: Conjunctive tuning may be sharpened within single P-ENs.
source: These observations suggest not only that tuning of P-EN output is strongly conjunctive, but also that this property may be sharpened within single P-ENs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of membrane potential and spike rate tuning shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Light level analysis of P-EN neuron morphology suggests that they likely have post-synaptic specializations in the bridge and pre-synaptic boutons in the ellipsoid body.
source: Light level analysis of P-EN neuron morphology suggests that they likely have post-synaptic specializations in the bridge and pre-synaptic boutons in the ellipsoid body, while E-PG morphology indicates the opposite polarity (Wolff et al., 2015), making it possible for the two cell types to be mutually connected.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to anatomical analysis from Wolff et al., 2015.

claim: E-PG morphology indicates post-synaptic specializations in the ellipsoid body and pre-synaptic boutons in the bridge.
source: Light level analysis of P-EN neuron morphology suggests that they likely have post-synaptic specializations in the bridge and pre-synaptic boutons in the ellipsoid body, while E-PG morphology indicates the opposite polarity (Wolff et al., 2015), making it possible for the two cell types to be mutually connected.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to anatomical analysis from Wolff et al., 2015.

claim: Light level analysis of brains in which HA-tagged synaptotagmin was expressed in P-EN neurons revealed stronger labeling in the ellipsoid body and noduli than in the bridge (11/14 brains).
source: Light level analysis of brains in which HA-tagged synaptotagmin was expressed in P-EN neurons revealed stronger labeling in the ellipsoid body and noduli than in the bridge (Figure 7A, 11/14 brains).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Analysis of the E-PG targeted brains revealed high levels of HA-tagged synaptotagmin in the protocerebral bridge, but also in the ellipsoid body.
source: In contrast, analysis of the E-PG targeted brains revealed high levels of HA-tagged synaptotagmin in the protocerebral bridge, but also in the ellipsoid body (at higher levels than in the ellipsoid body in 5/15 brains, at comparable levels in both neuropils in 10/15 brains, see Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of P-EN neurons reliably evoked positive calcium transients in E-PG neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of P-EN neurons reliably evoked positive calcium transients in E-PG neurons (Figure 7C, see Materials and methods), suggesting that angular velocity information is indeed relayed to E-PGs via this pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional connectivity experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Activation of the E-PG population induced more variable responses in P-ENs.
source: However, activation of the E-PG population induced more variable responses in P-ENs.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional connectivity experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Strong light intensities for optogenetic activation of E-PGs evoked responses consistent with excitatory connections in P-ENs.
source: Although we observed responses consistent with excitatory connections when we used strong light intensities for optogenetic activation (Figure 7D), the same pairing evoked activation, inhibition, and a lack of response at different times with weaker light intensities (dotted line in Figure 7D, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional connectivity experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The excitatory loop between E-PG and P-EN neurons may be both direct and indirect.
source: Thus, the excitatory loop between E-PG and P-EN neurons may be both direct and indirect, and the connection from the E-PG neurons onto the P-EN neurons likely also recruits inhibition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the variable responses observed in functional connectivity experiments.

claim: The connection from the E-PG neurons onto the P-EN neurons likely also recruits inhibition.
source: Thus, the excitatory loop between E-PG and P-EN neurons may be both direct and indirect, and the connection from the E-PG neurons onto the P-EN neurons likely also recruits inhibition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the variable responses observed in functional connectivity experiments.

claim: Imaging in the protocerebral bridge revealed two bumps of activity in the E-PG and P-EN neurons, one on each side of the bridge.
source: Imaging in the protocerebral bridge revealed two bumps of activity in the E-PG and P-EN neurons, one on each side of the bridge (Figure 8B), as predicted by our working model.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: For both neuron types, the bump intensities, but not widths, increased with increasing angular velocity across trials.
source: For both neuron types, the bump intensities, but not widths, increased with increasing angular velocity across trials (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of two-color calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: The P-EN bump intensity increased for both turn directions, but the increase was larger for ipsilateral turns than for contralateral turns.
source: Although the P-EN bump intensity increased for both turn directions, which was unexpected, the increase was larger for ipsilateral turns than for contralateral turns (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, top), a mirror-symmetry consistent with imaging results in the noduli (Figure 2) and with single cell electrophysiology (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was no difference between E-PG activity for ipsilateral versus contralateral turns at any turn velocity.
source: Consistent with our model, in which E-PG neurons carry the heading representation to the protocerebral bridge (Figure 1H), and in contrast with the activity of the P-EN subpopulations, there was no difference between E-PG activity for ipsilateral versus contralateral turns at any turn velocity (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The registered E-PG and P-EN activity bumps overlapped, but with the P-EN bumps slightly lagging the E-PG bumps.
source: Across velocities, the registered E-PG and P-EN activity bumps overlapped, but with the P-EN bumps slightly lagging the E-PG bumps (Figure 8E,G, see Materials and methods for further details on the registration and binning procedures).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of two-color calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8E,G.

claim: The lag led to bump offsets of approximately one glomerulus (the equivalent of 45 degrees in the ellipsoid body) at 120–150°/s.
source: The lag led to bump offsets of approximately one glomerulus (the equivalent of 45 degrees in the ellipsoid body) at 120–150°/s, the fastest rotational velocity bin considered (and the bin with the greatest offset), whether measured by the population vector average or by peak difference (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Bumps of activity were observed in both E-PG and P-EN neural populations in the ellipsoid body.
source: As in the protocerebral bridge, we observed bumps of activity in both neural populations (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Bump amplitudes, but not half-widths, varied with angular velocity in the ellipsoid body.
source: Bump amplitudes, but not half-widths, varied with angular velocity (Figure 9D,E), and both bumps were ~100° wide (full width at half maximum, Figure 9E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 9D,E.

claim: At angular velocities less than 30°/s, all flies showed bump offsets of less than 6° (2.5 ± 2.1°, N = 10 flies).
source: At angular velocities less than 30°/s, all flies showed bump offsets of less than 6° (2.5 ± 2.1°, N = 10 flies, Figure 9F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 9F,G.

claim: At rotational velocities above 30°/s, P-EN population activity separated from E-PG activity, with the P-EN bump leading the E-PG bump around the ellipse.
source: However, at rotational velocities above 30°/s, P-EN population activity separated from E-PG activity, with the P-EN bump leading the E-PG bump around the ellipse (Figure 9G, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9G and Video 2.

claim: When the red indicator was expressed in the E-PG neurons and the green indicator in the P-EN neurons, the bump offset exceeded 15 degrees of separation for turns faster than 90°/s (20.7 ± 11.7° at 150–180°/s).
source: When the red indicator was expressed in the E-PG neurons and the green indicator in the P-EN neurons, the bump offset exceeded 15 degrees of separation for turns faster than 90°/s regardless of turn direction and regardless of whether the fly was angularly accelerating or decelerating (20.7 ± 11.7° at 150–180°/s).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of two-color calcium imaging data.

claim: The P-EN bump leads the E-PG bump in the ellipsoid body during turns.
source: Thus, we concluded that the P-EN bump leads the E-PG bump in the ellipsoid body during turns, consistent with the conceptual model.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the two-color calcium imaging data.

claim: The firing rate model captured the essence of much of what was observed in experiments.
source: This rate model, which is reminiscent of past models of mammalian head direction cells (Skaggs et al., 1995; Xie et al., 2002; Zhang, 1996), albeit with key differences in connectivity, captured the essence of much of what we observed in our experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions to experimental data.

claim: Simulated firing rate curves of P-ENs in response to rotational velocity input were sigmoidal with an inflexion point at 0°/s, matching experimental observations.
source: Simulated firing rate curves of P-ENs in response to rotational velocity input were sigmoidal with an inflexion point at 0°/s, matching our experimental observations (compare Figure 10—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: The simulations indicated that the circuit functions as a ring attractor, enforcing a unique bump across the E-PG population.
source: Further, the simulations indicated that the circuit functions as a ring attractor, enforcing a unique bump across the E-PG population, consistent with previous experimental results (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015, Kim et al., 2017) (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations and comparison to prior experimental results.

claim: The persistent bump of activity arises from a feedback loop between E-PG and P-EN neural populations.
source: Our model does not feature an attractor network within the E-PG population. Rather, E-PG activity is driven entirely by P-EN neurons and the persistent bump of activity arises from a feedback loop between these two neural populations.
evidence: This claim is based on the structure of the firing rate model.

claim: The activity and bump amplitudes of both populations are sensitive to velocity input.
source: As a result, the activity and bump amplitudes of both populations are sensitive to velocity input, as observed experimentally (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions that match experimental observations.

claim: The firing rate model produced offsets in the activity of the E-PG and P-EN neurons in the ellipsoid body and in the protocerebral bridge, qualitatively matching experimental observations.
source: The firing rate model also produced offsets in the activity of the E-PG and P-EN neurons in the ellipsoid body and in the protocerebral bridge, qualitatively matching our experimental observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions to experimental data.

claim: In the simulations, the offsets are due to the neural time constants.
source: In the simulations, the offsets are due to the neural time constants (see Materials and methods); the bump in the P-EN population is not updated immediately after the E-PG bump shifts.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the firing rate model.

claim: The architecture of the model ensures a quasi-linear relationship between bump rotation and steady velocity input.
source: Indeed, the architecture of our model ensures a quasi-linear relationship between bump rotation and steady velocity input (Figure 10E) up to an inherent saturating angular velocity.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 10E.

claim: This linearity mainly depends on an appropriate balance of local E-PG to P-EN excitation, and inhibition onto the P-EN neurons.
source: This linearity mainly depends on an appropriate balance of local E-PG to P-EN excitation, and inhibition onto the P-EN neurons (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by model analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The bump in the model closely followed the integrated external velocity, reliably tracking the animal's heading.
source: When we drove the P-ENs with a simulated but realistic time varying velocity input (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), we saw that the bump in the model closely followed the integrated external velocity, reliably tracking the animal's heading (see Figure 10F, Figure 10—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 10F and Figure 10—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: At room temperature, the distribution of E-PG bump amplitude across trials was similar for the control flies and for flies that expressed shiTS in the P-EN neurons.
source: At room temperature, the distribution of E-PG bump amplitude across trials was similar for the control flies and for flies that expressed shiTS in the P-EN neurons (Figure 11D).
evidence: This claim is supported by shiTS experimental data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: At 31°C, when the flies became more active and increased their forward velocity, the amplitude distribution of the control flies shifted to higher values.
source: At 31°C, however, when the flies became more active and increased their forward velocity, the amplitude distribution of the control flies shifted to higher values.
evidence: This claim is supported by shiTS experimental data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: In the shiTS P-EN flies at 31°C, the bump amplitude distribution remained relatively unchanged, or even decreased.
source: In contrast, in the shiTS P-EN flies, where this activity increase was accompanied by a synaptic block in P-EN neurons, the bump amplitude distribution remained relatively unchanged, or even decreased (Figure 11D).
evidence: This claim is supported by shiTS experimental data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: The model demonstrated that two recurrent E-PG/P-EN loops are sufficient to maintain and shift a bump of activity.
source: The model demonstrated that two recurrent E-PG/P-EN loops are sufficient to maintain and shift a bump of activity (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 10.

claim: At higher P-EN to E-PG synaptic efficacies, network activity localized into a bump, and its amplitude increased as the efficacy of the synaptic connection between P-EN and E-PG neurons increased.
source: At higher P-EN to E-PG synaptic efficacies, network activity localized into a bump, and its amplitude increased as the efficacy of the synaptic connection between P-EN and E-PG neurons increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 11E.

claim: This critical role for the P-EN-to-E-PG connection in maintaining bump strength was consistent with the reduction in bump amplitude observed experimentally when P-EN output was impaired.
source: This critical role for the P-EN-to-E-PG connection in maintaining bump strength was consistent with the reduction in bump amplitude that we observed experimentally across flies and genotypes when P-EN output was impaired (Figure 11D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions to shiTS experimental data.

claim: R2 values for the correlation of changes in heading versus PVA were, on average, lower for the P-EN lines than for the control line.
source: These R2 values were, on average, lower for the P-EN lines than for the control line, suggesting that disrupting the P-EN synaptic output affects the reliability of the E-PG bump to track turns.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of shiTS experimental data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Disrupting the P-EN synaptic output affects the reliability of the E-PG bump to track turns.
source: These R2 values were, on average, lower for the P-EN lines than for the control line, suggesting that disrupting the P-EN synaptic output affects the reliability of the E-PG bump to track turns.
evidence: This claim is inferred from statistical analysis of shiTS experimental data.

claim: P-EN activity is important for maintaining the E-PG bump's strength and stability.
